appraisal_events.evidence: pour se montrer royal jusqu'au bout... donna l'ordre d'apporter du champagne... celui du père était l'avarice. Aussi, c'est dans une carafe qu'il fit servir sous le nom de champagne un petit vin mousseux et sous celui de fauteuils d'orchestre il avait fait prendre des parterres qui coûtaient moitié moins
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator ironically exposes Bloch père's staged munificence (champagne, orchestra seats) as a sham concealing his stinginess, deflating his pretension to grandeur.

appraisal_events.evidence: quel était cet excellent fantoche... une impayable bobine de gaga de la plus haute lignée... [then, learning it is Saint-Loup's aristocratic uncle] je mettrais en relief le côté aristocratique de votre oncle, qui en somme fait un effet boeuf... frappe par un très grand style
appraisal_events.explanation: Bloch's mockery of the man he saw on the beach flips instantly into fawning admiration once he learns the man is an aristocrat, exposing his opportunistic, status-driven inconsistency.

appraisal_events.evidence: elle recula de quelques pas, tant furent grandes sa stupeur et sa déception... « Comment, c'est cela, Bloch ! »... comme si un personnage aussi prestigieux eût dû posséder une apparence qui « fît connaître » immédiatement qu'on se trouvait en présence d'un grand de la terre
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator gently mocks Françoise's naive assumption that reputation must show in appearance, ironizing her credulous social reasoning, while also noting her underlying good nature ('elle eut la bonté d'ajouter').

status_effects.explanation: His performed generosity is unmasked as petty deception, diminishing him in the narrator's ironic portrayal.
His abrupt reversal from mockery to flattery upon learning of aristocratic connection reveals opportunistic snobbery, ironized by the narrator.
Her naive, reputation-based social judgment is gently ironized, though tempered by an acknowledgment of her good will.

ambiguities: In parts of the passage, unqualified 'Bloch' could plausibly refer to either the father or the son; the theatre outing, the Charlus exchange, and the Odette boast are read here as involving the son (young Bloch), consistent with his established role as the narrator's companion, while the dinner-table generosity/avarice material is read as the father's.

Bloch's crude boast of intimacy with the 'belle personne' (implicitly Odette) is presented as his own dubious, self-serving claim, undercut by the narrator's skeptical silence; this was not scored as a discredit event on Odette given the unreliability of its source.
